name: Tamil
signature: Curvy and loopy with flat top-bars on many letters, repeated arches, and no continuous head-line.
combination: A consonant carries an inherent 'a' (க = ka). A vowel sign replaces that vowel (க + ா → கா = kā). The puḷḷi ் — a DOT above the letter — removes the vowel entirely (க் = k). Unlike Devanagari, Tamil does NOT fuse the bare consonant into a conjunct: the dot stays visible and both letters keep their full shape. (A handful of Sanskrit-borrowed ligatures are the exception — க்ஷ kṣa and ஸ்ரீ śrī.)
notes: Used by Tamil in this curriculum. The inventory below covers the greeting and self-introduction vocabulary of Chapters 1–2 and grows from there; it is deliberately not the full 247-character grid. Stroke orders are the common handwriting convention, not a standard — Tamil is taught with regional and school-to-school variation. IMPORTANT for authors: a `strokeOrder` list names the PARTS of a letter in writing order; it does NOT by itself say where the pen lifts. The same holds for the sources: the numbered hand-movement arrows in Radhakrishnan's Appendix I, the numbered parts of a writing diagram, and the frames of an animated GIF mark movements and changes of direction, and none of them is evidence of a pen lift. Count a lift only on explicit evidence, such as the pen tip jumping in an animation, a second start dot, or a written instruction to lift. Native Tamil writers draw most letters in one continuous stroke: in HP Labs India's online handwriting data (the LipiTk 4.0 Tamil isolated-character recognizer, trained on hpl-tamil-iso-char), 85–99% of the stored prototypes of each base consonant are a single pen-down stroke. All thirty letters in this starter inventory have authored, font-checked pen paths (`DUCTUS` in language-ladder's `strokes.ts`). க, ச, ஞ, ண, த, ந, ர, ழ, ள, ற, and ன are each one continuous stroke: the manual's numbered movements followed in order without lifting, retracing shared ink where the next movement starts elsewhere (each record says where). The independent vowels இ, ஐ, ஒ, and ஓ are one continuous stroke in the same way, and ஊ is two: உ without lifting, one lift, then ள without lifting, as Module 17 builds it. உ, ட, ப, ம, ய, வ, and ல are also each a single unbroken stroke even though their parts have separate names, and ஏ is a single six-movement run through its hooked diagonal foot. அ, ஆ, எ, ங, and ஷ are one continuous stroke too, on the counts in the same HP Labs data (91%, 97%, 92%, 85%, and 93% of their stored prototypes; counts and shares only, no trace copied). அ and ஆ follow Frame 4 in order and climb the right upright from the end of the horizontal before drawing it down, so the old lift before the upright is gone. எ and ங follow the native writers' order instead of the manual's, and each record says where it overrides it: எ starts inside its bowl, goes clockwise round it, up the left side and along the top bar, and draws the right upright down last (Frame 5 started on the outer left side and drew the upright upward after a lift); ங goes down its left upright and back up, along the top bar, down the inner stem, round the bowl and along the low bar, and draws the right upright upward last (Frame 2 drew that upright first, as a detached part). ஷ follows Narale's four numbered parts in his order without lifting; his chart numbers parts, which is not evidence of a lift. Where the print face carries a bar past an upright or leaves a free foot, the path runs out and back over that ink, and each record says so. Only ஊ keeps a lift, between its உ and its ள, as 93% of its prototypes do. ஸ, the thirtieth, is cited straight to the LipiTk Tamil recognizer's native-writer prototypes (counts and shares only): one continuous stroke that goes back up its stem once. Component descriptions name the pieces a learner can see in the vendored Noto Sans Tamil face; several letters share a straight top bar and are best learned as a family (ச/க, ண/ன, ந, ர, ற).
